3.0.s.en: 1. Fatherhood and sonship in the Lord

3.0.0.en: 1 The sons of wisdom are the assembly of the righteous, and their offspring are the people of obedience and love. 2 O my children, hear the words of your father, and do them, that you may be saved. 3 For the Lord has honored the father over the children, and has confirmed the judgment of the mother over the sons. 4 He who honors his father atones for his sins, and refrains from them, and is heard in the prayer of every day. 5 And he who respects his mother is like one who lays up treasures. 6 He who honors his father rejoices in his children, and in the day of his prayer he is heard. 7 He who respects his father will have long days, and he who obeys his father gives rest to his mother. 8 He who fears the Lord honors his parents, and serves his parents as masters to him.

3.0.1.en: When he speaks of the holy family, he regards his school as a family that has its role in the life of society. He calls his students his sons, at times in the plural, a sign of the unity of the students with one another and of his relationship to them as a father, and at times he speaks in the singular: "My son." He desires to walk in the Spirit of God, who deals with the community, whether leaders or people, as all being the people of God, the object of His love and special care. At the same time he sees in each son a special member who has his own special place in his father's heart.

3.0.2.en: He also made clear the secret of the concern for fatherhood or motherhood and sonship:

3.0.3.en: a. "And do what I tell you, that you may be saved" [1]. The love translated into fatherhood and sonship is the way of salvation. For the heaven prepared for us has love as its law, and whoever does not practice love for God and people does not enjoy it.

3.1.0.en: b. This love is in truth a divine commandment; every honor given to parents the Lord counts as honor given to Himself, and it is a right that they receive through the divine commandment [2].

3.2.0.en: c. Every honor directed to them opens for us the door of God's mercies, so that we receive forgiveness of our sins, and every care for the mother and glorification of her is a credit for the son or daughter, kept as a treasure in heaven [4].

3.3.0.en: d. What we offer to our parents is repaid to us later by our children, and it lifts up our prayers here, while we are in the world, as on two wings to heaven [5].

3.3.1.en: e. Whoever honors his parents, the Lord blesses every minute of his life, so his life is lengthened through the divine blessing, and the Lord makes each day of his days as a thousand years (2 Pet 3:8).

3.3.2.en: f. It befits children not to be ashamed of serving their parents; whoever honors his parents according to the flesh is counted as an offering to the heavenly Father and to the Church, his spiritual mother, and therefore he serves them as masters to him.

3.3.3.en: In brief, the Lord Himself looks upon the family as the church of the holy home.

3.3.4.en: He also made clear the secret of the concern for fatherhood or motherhood and sonship:

3.3.5.en: My children, listen to me, your father, and do what I tell you, that you may be saved [1].

3.3.6.en: When Sirach calls himself a father to his students and regards them as his sons, he only affirms that the constitution of the family rests on mutual love and on concern for the salvation of all its members. What concerns him is not that they should occupy distinguished positions in society, nor that they should be trained to conduct dialogues in a certain manner, but that all should work for salvation.

3.3.7.en: * The Lord taught us not only to take no thought about anything concerning our possessions and the necessities of this life, but also to rise above natural feelings, when He said: "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" (Mt 10:37). This applies also to deep ties such as close friendships. How much more, then, to distant relations and to those who are strangers to the faith. Therefore He added: "And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me" (Mt 10:38). The Apostle, who succeeded in this, writes to us: "the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world... I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 6:14; 2:20).

3.3.8.en: Let us return to the words of the Lord that He spoke directly to each one of us. When that man asked Him, saying: "Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father," He answered him: "Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God" (Lk 9:59-60). And that other who said to Him: "Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house," He answered him with rebuke and reproof, saying: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God" (Lk 9:61-62)...

3.3.9.en: He wants us to refrain from hearing any voice that makes us turn aside from the way of perfection and godliness... For He says: "Whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple" (Lk 14:27). We do this when we pass through the waters of Baptism, where we declare our faith and confess that we were crucified with Christ and died and were buried with Him... as it is written (see Rom 6:4-11)[1].

3.3.10.en: St. Basil the Great For the Lord honored the father over his children, and confirmed the right of the mother over her sons [2].

3.3.11.en: Whoever honors his father atones for his sins [3].

3.3.12.en: And whoever glorifies his mother is like one who lays up treasures [4].

3.3.13.en: Whoever honors his parents expects God to hear his prayer, just as he expects that his children will honor him.

3.3.14.en: Whoever honors his father will rejoice in his children, and when he prays he is heard [5].

3.3.15.en: When the Holy Bible speaks of the father, it usually means the parents; there is no distinction between fathers and mothers.

3.4.0.en: Whoever exalts his father will have a long life, and whoever obeys the Lord gives rest to his mother [6].

3.5.0.en: The Holy Bible links obedience to the Lord with obedience to parents. By honoring our parents we receive the blessing of obedience to the divine commandment (Deut 28:1-2). Kindness to parents helps in the forgiveness of sins, and contempt for parents is counted as blasphemy against God [16].

3.5.1.en: Obedience to parents does not stop at children and youth, for it also befits the person who reaches adulthood to honor his parents, and so receive the blessing of the Lord. At the same time his work returns to him, as his children honor him and obey him. It is stated in this book:

3.5.2.en: And serves his parents as masters to him [7].

3.5.3.en: Those who fear the Lord serve their parents with joy. It befits them to help them in their old age and to be gentle with them if they lose their reason.

3.6.s.en: 2. The blessing of obedience and honoring parents

3.6.0.en: 9 Honor your father in deed and word, with all patience, 10 that a blessing may come upon you from him, and his blessing remain to the end. 11 For the blessing of the father establishes the houses of the children, and the curse of the mother uproots their foundations. 12 Do not glory in the dishonor of your father, for the dishonor of your father is no glory to you, 13 but a man's glory is the honor of his father, and the disgrace of the mother is a reproach to the children.

3.6.1.en: Honor your father in word and deed, that a blessing may come upon you from him [8].

3.6.2.en: Every honor that a person gives to his parents is counted as seed that he sows, to reap it later. This commandment is the only one stated among the Ten Commandments together with the blessings that it carries. "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee" (Ex 20:13).

3.6.3.en: The Holy Bible gave attention to this divine commandment, to which a divine promise is attached, so Ben Sirach cites it here [8-11] at some length, perhaps because some young people were drawn by philosophy away from attachment to the Law, so they despised the older generation, especially their parents, and considered themselves more advanced and more knowledgeable.

3.6.4.en: In the New Testament the Apostle Paul cited the same commandment: "Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise; that it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth" (Eph 6:2-3). And after the Flood, the first curse that fell upon man in the new world was because of Ham's dishonor of his father Noah (Gen 9:20-27).

3.6.5.en: The Jewish rabbis say, in commenting on the commandment "Honour thy father and thy mother," that before the Babylonian captivity the relationship between parents and children had in general worsened, so that Israel deserved to fall under captivity because it did not keep that commandment, which is tied to a long stay in the Promised Land. And the New Testament conveys to us a sorrowful picture of this denial on the part of children, for in the Gospel of our teacher Matthew it is stated: "Whosoever shall say to his father or his mother, It is a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; and honour not his father or his mother" (Mt 15:5). And in the Gospel of our teacher Mark: "If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother" (Mk 7:11-12). This tradition is commandments of men, contradicting the divine commandment for one purpose or another, like the example that the Lord Christ gave. For the sake of personal benefit the Jewish leaders laid down a commandment bearing the appearance of outward giving while hiding a breaking of the divine Law. For instance, a son could deprive his parents of their rights, not supporting them under the pretext that what he would pay them he offers as an offering to God, so he breaks the commandment of honoring parents, and is like one who cursed them by his deeds, and this is harsher than reviling with the tongue, for he deprives them of the right to a dignified life, and brings them into hardship of living under the cover of giving to the Temple. As Origen says: [When the fathers hear that what should be given to them has become part of the offering devoted to God, they refrain from taking it from their sons, even if they are in great need of the necessities of life.] And he says: [That the Pharisees were lovers of money (Lk 6:14), so they pretended to collect it to give to the poor, depriving the parents of the gifts of their children.]

3.6.6.en: For the blessing of the father establishes the houses of the children, and the curse of the mother uproots their foundations [9].

3.7.0.en: Do not glory in the dishonor of your father, for the dishonor of your father is no glory to you [10].

3.7.1.en: * "Do not glory in the dishonor of your father" (3:10). If this is said about our fathers according to nature, how much more about our spiritual fathers. Honor him because he serves you every day, and makes you read the Holy Bible, prepares the house for you, and guards you, and prays for you. He intercedes before God on your behalf, and offers supplications for you; all his worship is for your sake. To value all this, think on this, and draw near to him with godly reverence.

3.7.2.en: Do not say: He is wicked... The gifts that God gives are not based on the virtue of the priest. All His gifts are from His grace. The role of the priest is merely to open his mouth, and God is the One who does everything[2].

3.7.3.en: St. John Chrysostom Fulgentius feared that virgins might fall into pride and haughtiness toward their families because of their virginity.

3.7.4.en: * Just as lust has no power over the body of a virgin, so do not give pride power over the heart of a virgin. Work out your salvation in fear and trembling. For God works in you, that you may will and do His good will.

3.8.0.en: But a man's glory is the honor of his father, and the dishonor of the mother is a disgrace to the children [11].

3.9.s.en: 3. Bearing with the weaknesses of parents

3.9.0.en: 14 My son, help your father in his old age, and do not grieve him in his life. 15 And if his mind fails, bear with him, and do not despise him while you are in your full strength, for mercy shown to a father will not be forgotten. 16 And by bearing with the failings of your mother you will be repaid with good. 17 And upon your righteousness a house will be built for you, and you will be remembered in the day of your affliction, and like ice in fair weather your sins will be dissolved. 18 Whoever forsakes his father is like a blasphemer, and whoever provokes his mother is cursed by the Lord.

3.9.1.en: If one of the parents is afflicted with the weakness of old age, or with illness, or with loss of memory, the son regards this as by God's permission, so instead of murmuring he shows compassion to them. This tenderness has its effectiveness:

3.9.2.en: a. Sirach says of it that it is not forgotten [14]; it is a credit for the son with God, who hastens his deliverance in time of affliction.

3.9.3.en: b. It helps the son to atone for his sins; Ben Sirach likens it to the sun that melts the ice in fair weather.

3.9.4.en: My son, help your father in his old age, and do not grieve him in his life [12].

3.9.5.en: In an agricultural society the son can contribute to the work of sowing, as well as to tending the sheep.

3.9.6.en: And if he loses his mind, show compassion, and do not despise him while you are in all your strength [13].

3.9.7.en: For kindness to a father is not forgotten, and it counts toward atoning for your sins [14].

3.10.0.en: The day of your affliction will be remembered to your benefit, and like ice in fair weather your sins melt away [15].

3.10.1.en: When Ben Sirach spoke of the blessings of honoring parents, he lifted our hearts to God our heavenly Father, that we may enjoy His surpassing care. We honor our heavenly Father by offering Him a sacrifice of thanksgiving, especially in time of affliction, a sign of our faith and our trust in His care for us in the midst of affliction. The fruit of this thanksgiving is that it helps us to atone for our sins, that we may live by the righteousness of Christ.

3.10.2.en: "The day of your affliction will be remembered to your benefit, and like ice in fair weather your sins melt away." What a joyful comparison, for thanksgiving in affliction brings us into the clear light of day, and the Sun of righteousness melts our sins and removes them.

3.10.3.en: * What shall I render to You, O Lord? For when my memory recalls these things (the afflictions), I shall not be frightened by them!

3.10.4.en: I love You, O Lord, and I thank You, and I confess to Your name!

3.10.5.en: For You remove from me my evil, terrifying and malicious deeds.

3.10.6.en: I ascribe to Your grace and mercy that You melt my sins like snow[3].

3.10.7.en: St. Augustine St. Augustine sees our sins as resembling the ice that melts and dissolves by the work of the Holy Spirit. [We became frozen in captivity, our sins bind us, but when the south wind (the warm one) blows, that is, the Holy Spirit, He forgives our sins, and we come down from the ice of iniquity. For just as snow melts in warm weather, so also do our sins.[4]]

3.11.0.en: Whoever forsakes his father is like a blasphemer, and whoever provokes his mother is cursed by the Lord [16].

3.12.s.en: 4. The family is a school of meekness

3.12.0.en: 19 My son, conduct your affairs with meekness, and the good man will love you. 20 The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord. 21 For the power of the Lord is great, and by the humble He is glorified. 22 Do not seek what is too hard for you to attain, nor search out what is beyond your power, but what God has commanded you, meditate upon it, and do not desire to investigate His many works. 23 For you have no need to see hidden things with your eyes, 24 and what goes beyond your works, do not be overly concerned with it. 25 For you have been shown many things that exceed the understanding of man. 26 And many have been led astray by their presumption, and a corrupt fancy has made their minds slip. 27 The hard heart will end in evil, and he who loves danger will fall into it. 28 The heart that goes in two ways will not prosper, and the perverse of heart will stumble in both. 29 The hard heart is burdened with hardships, and the sinner adds sin to sin. 30 The disease of the proud has no cure, for the root of evil has taken root in him. 31 The heart of the intelligent ponders a proverb, and the desire of the wise is a listening ear. 32 The wise and intelligent heart refrains from sins, and prospers in works of righteousness.

3.12.1.en: When the Word of God became incarnate and dwelt among us as one of us, He called us to learn from Him, saying: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 11:29). Marriage and family life rest on the divine plan, and on the realization of God's plan for family life and for each member of the family. Through holy family life in the Lord, society comes to walk in harmony with God's plan, fulfilling its mission.

3.12.2.en: Ben Sirach gives us practical touches for a life of meekness and humility, for the believer to live in his small family as well as in society, which is the greater family.

3.13.0.en: The most beautiful offering with which parents are pleased is the humility and meekness of their children. The more the son humbles himself in his conduct toward them, the more he grows in greatness in the eyes of God and people. God is glorified in the humble person, because he knows his weakness and trusts in God, who raises up the weak as a hero (see Joel 3:10). The believer does not seek visions and the working of wonders and miracles; what concerns him is walking according to the divine commandment [21-22].

3.14.0.en: As the eye must be opened in order to receive the light [25], so the mind ought to be opened to receive wisdom (Prov 28:14).

3.14.1.en: a. Meekness does not stop at certain words or particular behaviors, but ought to be blended into and shine forth in all the works of the believer [17].

3.14.2.en: b. The believer does not seek worldly honor, but whenever he receives honor or authority or success in his works he ought to grow in humility, counting what he receives as free gifts from God, so he finds favor with the Lord, and honor even from people [18].

3.14.3.en: c. The believer ought not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think (Rom 12:3), but to recognize the truth of his abilities and capacities. So he does not seek what is beyond him, nor search into hidden matters through useless theoretical, disputatious dialogues [21-24]. When Pope Athanasius was asked by a person to show him his God so that he might believe in Him, he answered him: "Show me your spirit, and I will show you my God!"

3.14.4.en: d. Beware of falling into intellectual stubbornness.

3.14.5.en: My son, conduct your affairs with meekness, and the people whom the Lord approves will love you [17].

3.14.6.en: The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord [18].

3.14.7.en: If the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, then arrogance is the beginning of folly. Ben Sirach had in mind what pride had done, not only to individuals but also to nations, for Assyria fell, then Babylon, then Persia. He also lived through the fall of Carthage in 201 BC.

3.14.8.en: Humility is the disposition fitting for those who fear the Lord, who honor their parents. The more a person receives honor, whether on the ecclesiastical or the worldly level, the more he needs to double his humility, so that he may become the object of God's pleasure and not of people's approval. The archbishops used to fear pride lest they lose their salvation. So St. John Chrysostom would repeat in the depths of his heart, as among the bishops, his famous saying: "I marvel at a bishop who is saved!" At the beginning of the celebrations of the ordination of Pope Shenouda, he would sometimes open his speech by repeating what Chrysostom said, so that words of praise might not distract him from his eternity. The saying of our beloved father Fr. Bishoy Kamel is: The servant of church education is the servant of the children of his Master, and the priest is the servant of the servants, the children of their Master; how much more must this be the feeling of the bishop and the patriarch.

3.14.9.en: What grieves our hearts is that a priest thinks he is the head of the Church and that what he says must be obeyed without dialogue, and likewise the bishop and the patriarch.

3.14.10.en: * Often the ecclesiastical order and the Levitical work are a cause of falling into pride for one who forgets that he received this honor in the bosom of the Church.

3.14.11.en: How many men of the priesthood, when they became head, forgot that they must be humble, as though their ordination had exempted them from humility. On the contrary, they must keep humility carefully, because they are granted such great honor, according to the saying of Scripture: The greatest among you, let him be the most humble.

3.14.12.en: The community chooses you, so bow your head in greater humility. It has chosen you as a leader of others, so do not feel that you are glorified! Be among them as one of them (Lk 22:27). You must be humble and meek. Flee from pride, the source of all evils[5].

3.14.13.en: * The evil one fights us not only that we should commit sin with persistence..., but that we should be proud and feel that we are perfect. But God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Prov 34:3; Jas 6:4; 1 Pet 5:5). Therefore the more you humble yourself, the more you are lifted up and find mercy with God [18]...

3.14.14.en: Whoever turns aside from the commandment does not follow it, since the commandment of God is upright. "Cursed are they that turn aside from thy commandments" does not refer only to those who do not work them, but even to those who deviate from them a little.

3.14.15.en: Origen * "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me" (Ps 131:1). Let us say this more clearly, and be heard. I am not proud. I did not wish to be known among people for wonderful powers, and I did not seek anything beyond my strength. In this I boast among the foolish... May no man be proud of God's gift to him, but keep humility, and so fulfill what is written: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord" [18]. How much fear is needed of pride in God's gift. We must press ourselves more and more[6].

3.14.16.en: St. Augustine * Let our glory be in humility, and our boasting in not loving (vain) glory. And let our desire be in those things that please God and satisfy Him, keeping in our minds what the Wise Man says to us: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord" (Sir 3:18). For He rejects the proud, and regards the arrogant as His enemies. But the meek and the humble in heart He crowns with honors[7].

3.14.17.en: St. Cyril the Great For the power of the Lord is great, and the humble glorify Him [19].

3.14.18.en: Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power [20].

3.14.19.en: Pride reaches its extreme when a person becomes arrogant through his philosophical studies, and does not take into account that the gift of the mind is from God. With all its wonderful greatness, he realizes that it is limited and cannot come to know the mysteries of the Unlimited, nor His plan, without enjoying the work of His divine grace.

3.14.20.en: It befits us to seek wisdom and to grow in the knowledge of it, without relying on mere rational thought, for God, who treasures man as His ambassador on earth, does not withhold knowledge from him, but offers him what is for his edification according to man's capacities, and also reveals to him His divine will.

3.14.21.en: The danger that Sirach feared was that there had seeped into the holy land a disregard for the word of God and an indifference to the will of God, through Hellenistic ideas. This atmosphere created Jewish leaders who were arrogant in their thoughts and conduct.

3.14.22.en: * Deep meditation on the good life and care for the soul beget good people who love God.

3.14.23.en: Whoever seeks God finds Him, by overcoming all lusts through constant prayer. Such a person does not fear the demons[8].

3.14.24.en: St. Anthony the Great St. Ambrose presents Arius as an example of one who claims to be possessed of knowledge in what goes beyond human ability.

3.14.25.en: * It was said to Arius and to all men: "Do not seek what is far too hard for you." Moses was forbidden to see the face of God (Ex 33:23), and Arius thought he was qualified to see Him in a mystery... Paul speaks of lower matters: "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part" (1 Cor 13:9). But Arius says: "I know God with full knowledge, and not in part." Thus Paul is less than Arius. The chosen vessel knows in part, and the vessel of destruction knows all. Paul says: "I knew a man... whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth; how that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words" (2 Cor 12:3-4). Paul was carried up to the third heaven and did not know himself, while Arius wallows in filth and knows God.

3.14.26.en: Paul says of himself: "God knoweth," and Arius says of God: "I know"[9].

3.14.27.en: St. Ambrose Meditate on what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things [21].

3.14.28.en: * The Holy Bible warns us: "Meditate on what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things" [22]. "Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power" [21]. Of course we cannot use words that ascribe vain curiosity to the Holy Spirit. We must only say that searching into the hidden matters of God is a portion of his nature[10].

3.14.29.en: St. Epiphanius, Bishop of Salamis * Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power [20]. This does not mean that these matters are forbidden to us, for the Lord says: "There is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; and hid, that shall not be known" (Mt 10:26). But if we continue in the way we have undertaken, as the Apostle tells us, God will not only reveal to us what we do not know and ought to know, but will reveal whatever we care to know (Phil 3:15).

3.14.30.en: The way we have undertaken is the way of faith. May we keep it without hesitation. May it bring us into the mysteries of the King, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3)...

3.14.31.en: It befits us to proceed in progress and growth until our hearts become qualified and receive what we are unable to receive now. And if we find, on the last day, that we have advanced sufficiently, then we shall learn what we cannot know here[11].

3.14.32.en: St. Augustine Do not meddle in (searching) what goes beyond your works, for what has been revealed to you exceeds the understanding of man [22].

3.14.33.en: What is it that goes beyond your work? Searching into what cannot be comprehended, such as the essence of God or even the essence of the human soul.

3.14.34.en: * We read in Isaiah about Christ: "Who shall declare his generation?" (see Isa 53:8). When the blessed prophet speaks of God the Word, he uses the word "generation" instead of saying "essence" or "being." In truth, who can declare the being of the Only-Begotten Son? And what language can explain the unspeakable begetting of the Son from the Father? And what mind does not stand helpless and powerless before this concept? In truth we know and believe that the Word was begotten of God the Father. But we say that to entertain any question about this matter in discussion is extremely dangerous... We must not search into matters that exceed our mind and knowledge, not for us alone but for every creature, including those who are spirits[12].

3.14.35.en: St. Cyril the Great * God has not made all things revealed to you, nor has He permitted all things to be unknown to you. For He does not permit all things to be unknown to you, lest you say that the things that exist are not from (divine) providence. Nor does He permit all things to be known to you, lest the greatness of your knowledge stir up pride in you. So, at least, the wicked Satan pushed the first man to recklessness through the hope of greater knowledge, stripping him of the knowledge that he already had. Therefore the Wise Man advises us, saying: "Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into the things that exceed your power, but meditate with reverence on what you have been commanded, for the greater part of His works are done in secret" (see Sir 3:21-22)[13].

3.14.36.en: * "What has been shown to you exceeds the understanding of man" (Sir 3:22). But he says this for the consolation of the grieving, rebellious man, because he does not know everything. For even these things that (man) observes, and which he is permitted to know, are far greater than your understanding, since you could not attain them by yourself, but God taught them to you. Therefore be content with the wealth (in knowledge) that has been given to you and do not ask for more; rather give thanks for what you have received, and do not be angry about the things you have not received. Give glory for what you know, and do not stumble because of the things you do not know. For God made both equally profitable, and He reveals some things and hides others for the sake of your peace[14].

3.14.37.en: St. John Chrysostom Many have been led astray by their conclusions, and their evil suppositions made their thoughts slip and fall [23].

3.14.38.en: The stubborn heart ends in ruin, and he who loves danger perishes in it [24].

3.14.39.en: Fulgentius sees that the Wise Man is speaking here of the stubborn heretic, so he calls him to return to the Catholic Church, in which is the love that covers a multitude of sins through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

3.14.40.en: * Question: If one will fall under many blows, while another under few blows (Lk 12:47), how do some say that the punishment is infinite?

3.14.41.en: Answer: The things that were said in a veiled and obscure manner in certain places of the inspired book of God have been made clear in explicit terms in other places. The Lord declares once that these go away into eternal punishment (Mt 25:46), and again that He sends persons to the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Mt 5:22), and adds: "Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched (Mk 9:48), which the prophet said rightly long ago: "their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched" (Isa 66:24).

3.14.42.en: Since many such sayings are found everywhere in the inspired Holy Bible, this is certainly one of the strategies of Satan: that many people, by ignoring these valuable and weighty words and declarations of the Lord, reassure themselves that the punishment has an end, so that they may commit sin with great boldness. If there were an end to eternal torment, then surely life would not be eternal.

3.14.43.en: Now if we cannot bear to think in this way about eternity, by what logic is it possible to give eternal torment an end? The attribute "eternal" is attached equally to both elements. Therefore He says: "And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal" (Mt 25:46).

3.14.44.en: From the viewpoint of the explicit sayings, we must understand that those who are beaten with many blows, and those who are beaten with few blows, this does not mean an end to the torment, but points to different degrees.

3.14.45.en: If God is a just Judge, not only for the righteous but also for the wicked, who "will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:6), therefore one deserves an unquenchable fire, which can burn quietly or slowly, and another may deserve the worm that dieth not, and this can be moderate or great according to exactly what the person deserves.

3.14.46.en: A third may deserve Gehenna, in which there is a different kind of torment, while another deserves outer darkness (Mt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30), where all he does is weep, and another suffers gnashing of teeth because of excruciating pain. And outer darkness certainly indicates that there is also an inner darkness.

3.14.47.en: Moreover it is said in Proverbs about the depths of hell (Prov 9:18), which shows that some of those in hell are not in its depths, but receive less torment instead.

3.14.48.en: This can be clarified now by taking into consideration the condition of the body. One may suffer from fever with other symptoms and pains, while another suffers from fever but not like the former. And in another way a third, who differs from the first person, does not suffer from fever, being sick, but has pain in his limbs, which may be greater or less.

3.14.49.en: Now in the present case the "much" and "few" that the Lord spoke follow the customary style with different expressions. And for us this manner of speaking is applied to one afflicted with some illness, as we say in wonder concerning a person who suffers only from fever or from a sharp pain in his eyes: how long has he been suffering, or what troubles he suffers.

3.14.50.en: Again I say that punishment, severe or mild, is not related to the lengthening or shortening of time, but to the difference of the punishment[15].

3.14.51.en: St. Basil the Great The stubborn heart is burdened with pains, and the sinner adds sin to sin [25].

3.15.0.en: The disease of the proud has no cure, for the plant of evil has taken root in him [26].

3.15.1.en: Ben Sirach affirms the danger of stubbornness, which touches the depths of man before it appears in behavior; he attributes it to the heart as well as to the mind. If the fruit of stubbornness is ruin and deviation from sin to sin, he counts it as the root of a hidden plant which inevitably yields its bitter fruit in due time, and without ceasing. This stubbornness has no cure by a mere human decision to stop it, but needs grace, able to change and renew the thick and hardened heart (Mk 8:17; Heb 4:7).

3.15.2.en: The intelligent man reflects on the discourses of the wise, and makes his ears attentive to the voice of the Lord, so he enjoys with Moses the prophet the divine presence when he drew near to the bush burning with fire and not consumed, and through this presence came to know the mystery of the incarnation of the Word of God. The wise man sings in the spirit of humility with the Psalmist, saying: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me. Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child" (Ps 131:1-2).

3.15.3.en: * I am not proud: I do not wish to be known among people for wonderful powers, and I do not seek anything beyond my ability, of which I boast among the foolish. Like Simon the Magician, who wished to advance in wonders beyond his abilities, and therefore was the more pleased with the authority of the Apostles than with the righteousness of Christians[16].

3.15.4.en: St. Augustine The heart of the intelligent reflects on the proverb[17], and the attentive ear is the desire of the wise [27].

3.16.s.en: 5. The family is a school of giving

3.16.0.en: 33 Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins. 34 Whoever has done good is remembered in his latter end, and finds support in the day of his fall. Holy family life is a school of giving. 1. The doer of kindness and the giver of alms enjoys the compassion of God, who forgives sins, so he walks in safety because what he offers today supports him in the future in the midst of affliction (3:30-31). 2. Sirach urges us not to be slow in caring for the needy, so that we may practice our sonship to God, the lover of giving, and be the object of His love. God's love for the giver is greater than a mother's love for her son. 3. Whoever ignores the needs of the poor becomes a victim of the curse issuing from their sighs. 4. It befits us to respect all: the noble and the poor! 5. Whoever is given authority should realize that authority is a talent and a responsibility, and requires him to do justice to the oppressed. 6. God is the father of the orphan who has no father, and the judge of the widows who have no one to defend them (Ps 68:6).

3.16.1.en: Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins [28].

3.16.2.en: Ben Sirach regards almsgiving as like an ambassador who goes before a man, preparing the way for him to God, and sees it also as a credit for the believer that supports him in time of affliction and distress.

3.16.3.en: * After prayer with struggle there is a need for many almsdeeds, because these especially give power to the medicine of repentance. And just as among physicians there is a medicine made from many herbs, yet there is one medicine that is the main herb, indeed it is counted as though it were everything. Therefore hear what the Holy Bible says: "But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:41). And also: "By almsgiving and works of faith sins are purified" (Prov 16:6) LXX. And "Water quenches a flaming fire, almsgiving atones for great sins" (Sir 3:28)[18].

3.16.4.en: * What is said to the person whom a poor man provokes? To bear with the weaknesses of others, and to set the petitioner right before giving him the gift, by showing him gentle looks and kind words[19].

3.16.5.en: * Fasting brings us no little relief, and frees from entangled sins, on condition that the person devotes himself to showing compassion to others, and quenches the flame of God's wrath (1 Tim 2:1). For "Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins" (Sir 3:28)[20].

3.16.6.en: * Let us use every means to wash away defilement. But first the font washes, and after that there are many means of every kind. For God, being merciful, afterward (that is, after Baptism) provided various ways of reconciliation, the first among all of them being almsgiving. It is said: "By almsgiving and works of faith sins are atoned for" (see Sir 3:28)[21].

3.16.7.en: St. John Chrysostom Salvian, priest of Marseilles in the fifth century, reveals that giving in itself does not bestow eternal life, even if the person bequeaths the distribution of all that he has while at death's door, unless he walks in Christ Jesus in repentance.

3.16.8.en: * I do not think that wealth helps anyone if he lives continually in the pleasures of the body, or that he can obtain eternal life, unless he resists sin unto death; even if he bequeaths all that he has while at death's door, unless he truly gives up his sins, and takes off his defiled garments filled with his fornication, and puts on the garment of repentance and holiness from the hands of the Apostle who counsels him (Rom 2:5)[22].

3.16.9.en: Salvian, priest of Marseilles In one of his moral essays, St. Cyprian presents almsgiving and works of righteousness as another path to forgiveness after the forgiveness of sins in Baptism.

3.16.10.en: * The Holy Spirit speaks in the Holy Scriptures and says: "By almsgiving and faith iniquity is covered" (see Prov 16:6), and also says: "Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins" (Ben Sirach 3:33). Here it makes clear that just as the fire of Gehenna is quenched by the water of salvation, so by almsgiving and righteousness the flame of sins is put out (for those who believe in the blood of the Lord Christ). For since forgiveness of all sins is granted once in Baptism, the continuous work without interruption, following the example of Baptism, grants God's mercies again.

3.16.11.en: The Lord also taught us this in the Gospel, for when it was pointed out to the disciples that they eat without washing their hands, He answered, saying: "He that made that which is without made that which is within also. But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:40-41). He teaches the washing of the heart, not of the hands, and that rather the defilement of the inside is to be removed, not the filth of the outside, and that once the mind is purified, then a man begins to clean his body. And as He counsels us how to wash and be purified, He said that it is necessary to give alms.

3.16.12.en: That compassionate One teaches us and urges us to show kindness. For as He seeks the salvation of those for whom He offered a sacrifice of such measure, He pointed also to those who, after receiving the grace of Baptism and committing sin, can be cleansed anew[23].

3.16.13.en: The Martyr Cyprian * Some husbands scatter on the tombs of their wives violets, roses, lilies and purple flowers, and calm the grief of their hearts by performing this gentle duty. Our dear Pammachius watered the holy ashes and the venerated bones of Paulina, but in truth with the balsam of almsgiving. This is the sweet preparation and the perfumes by which the ashes of his dead wife are immortalized, knowing what is written: "Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins" [28][24].

3.16.14.en: St. Jerome * Why do the first inherit the kingdom? "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." Why do the others go to eternal fire? "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat."

3.16.15.en: I ask, what does this mean? I see that those who inherit the kingdom were given as good and faithful Christians, not despisers of the words of the Lord, having firm hope in the promises, so they did, for if they had not done so, that barrenness would not have accorded with their good life. They may be pure, not deceivers nor drunkards, keeping themselves from all works of evil, but they do not add to this good works and so remain barren. Because they wanted to be kept far from evil, "but they did not want to keep themselves, and do good" (Ps 34:14), yet He did not say even to these "Come, inherit the kingdom" because you lived pure and did not defraud anyone, nor wrong a poor man, nor trespass on anyone's boundary, nor deceive anyone with an oath. He did not say this, but He said "inherit the kingdom, for I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat."

3.16.16.en: O the distinction of this one above all the rest (of the virtues), for the Lord did not point to all but to it alone! Likewise He says to the others: "Depart ye into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."

3.16.17.en: How many things He could raise against the wicked when they ask: Why do we go to eternal fire? Why? Do you ask, O fornicators, murderers, deceivers, desecrators of temples, blasphemers and unbelievers? Yet He mentioned not one of these, but "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat."

3.16.18.en: I see you marveling as I do. And truly it is a marvelous matter. But I shall gather, as much as I can, the reasons for this marvelous matter, and I will hide nothing from you. It is written, "Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins" (Wisdom of Joshua 3:30), and it is also written: "Shut up alms in thy storehouses: and it shall deliver thee from all affliction" (Sir 29:12)[25].

3.16.19.en: St. Augustine * [In his praise of St. Paula, mother of Eustochium]

3.16.20.en: Many married women used to offer gifts to those who praise (the trumpet-blowers). While they spend excessively on a few, they close their hands on the many.

3.16.21.en: Paula was completely free from this error. She gave what she had to everyone according to his need, not according to her own desires, but to supply wants. No poor man left her empty-handed. She was able to do all this not because of the greatness of her wealth, but because of her wonderful management. Such phrases were always on her lips: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Mt 5:7).
